questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The projection of a line on a co-ordinate axes are $2,3,6$. Then the length of the line is
questions.solution:
Let $\mathbf{a}=a_1 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+a_2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+a_3 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$
Here, $\left(a_1 \hat{\mathbf{i}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{i}}=a_1=2 ;\left(a_2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{j}}=a_2=3$ and $\left(a_3 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{k}}=a_3=6\therefore \mathbf{a}=2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+6 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\text { Now, required length } \begin{aligned} & =|a|=\sqrt{2^2+3^2+6^2} \\ & =\sqrt{4+9+36}=\sqrt{49}=7 \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the point $(0,2,1)$ on a line passing through $(\alpha, 5,1)$ is $\left(\frac{5}{3}, \frac{7}{3}, \frac{15}{i}\right)$, then $\alpha$ is equal to _____
questions.solution:
It is given that point $Q\left(\frac{5}{3}, \frac{7}{3}, \frac{15}{4}\right)$ is foot of perpendicular of point $P(0,2,1)$ to a line passes through point $A(\alpha, 5,1)$. So, $P Q \perp A Q$.
$\because$ Direction ratios of line segments $P Q$ is $\left(\frac{5}{3}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{11}{4}\right)$ and direction ratios of line $A Q$ is $\left(\alpha-\frac{5}{3}, \frac{8}{3},-\frac{11}{4}\right)$. $\begin{array}{cc} \therefore & \frac{5}{3}\left(\alpha-\frac{5}{3}\right)+\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{8}{3}+\frac{11}{4} \times\left(-\frac{11}{4}\right)=0 \\ \Rightarrow & 15 \alpha-25+8+\frac{99(-11)}{16}=0 \\ \Rightarrow & 15 \alpha-17=\frac{99 \times 11}{16} \\ \Rightarrow & 5 \alpha=\frac{1089-817}{16} \\ \Rightarrow & 5 \alpha=54.466 \Rightarrow \alpha=10.893 \end{array}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{3}=\frac{z-1}{4}$ and $\frac{\boldsymbol{x}-3}{1}=\frac{\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{k}}{2}=\frac{z}{1}$ intersect, then $k$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given, two lines
$L_1: \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{3}=\frac{z-1}{4}$
and $L_2: \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-k}{2}=\frac{z-0}{1}$
Let $L_1: \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{3}=\frac{z-1}{4}=p$
and $L_2: \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-k}{2}=\frac{z-0}{1}=q$
Any point $P$ on line $L_1$ is of type
$P(2 p+1,3 p-1$ and $4 p+1)$ and any point $Q$ on the line $L_2$ is of type $Q(q+3,2 q+k$ and $q)$
Since, $L_1$ and $L_2$ are intersecting each other, hence, both point $P$ and $Q$ should coincide at the point of intersection. Corresponding co-ordinates of $P$ and $Q$ should be same.
$2 p+1=q+3,3 p-1=2 q+k \text { and } 4 p+1=q$
On solving, $2 p+1=q+3$ and $4 p+1=q$, we get
$p=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $q=-5$
On substituting the values of $p$ and $q$ in the third equation $3 p-1=2 q+k$, we get
$3\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)-1=2(-5)+k\therefore \quad k=\frac{9}{2}$

questions.q: If a line makes $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ with the positive direction of $x, y$ and $z$-axes respectively. Then, $\cos ^2 \alpha+\cos ^2 \beta+\cos ^2 \gamma$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ be the angles which the line makes with the positive directions at the axes of $x, y$ and $z$ respectively, then $\cos \alpha, \cos \beta$ and $\cos \gamma$ are called the direction cosines of the line and these are usually denoted by
$\begin{gathered}
l=\cos \alpha, m=\cos \beta, n=\cos \gamma \\
\therefore \cos ^2 \alpha+\cos ^2 \beta+\cos ^2 \gamma=l^2+m^2+n^2=1
\end{gathered}$

questions.q: If the lines $\frac{x-2}{1}=\frac{y-3}{1}=\frac{z-4}{-k}$ and $\frac{x-1}{2 k}=\frac{y-3}{2}=\frac{z-5}{1}$ are coplanar, then $k$ can have
questions.solution:
The given lines are
$\frac{x-2}{1}=\frac{y-3}{1}=\frac{z-4}{-k}$  ...(i)
and
$\frac{x-1}{2 k}=\frac{y-3}{2}=\frac{z-5}{1}$  ...(ii)
Condition for two lines are coplanar
$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
x_1-x_2 & y_1-y_2 & z_1-z_2 \\
l_1 & m_1 & n_1 \\
l_2 & m_2 & n_2
\end{array}\right|=0$
where $\left(x_1, y_1, z_1\right)$ and $\left(x_2, y_2, z_2\right)$ are points on lines (i) and (ii) and ( $\left.l_1, m_1, n_4\right)$ and $\left(l_2, m_2, n_2\right)$ are direction cosines of lines (i) and (ii), respectively.
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
2-1 & 3-3 & 4-5 \\
1 & 1 & -k \\
2 k & 2 & 1
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 0 & -1 \\
1 & 1 & -k \\
2 k & 2 & 1
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 1(1+2 k)-0-1(2-2 k)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 1+2 k-2+2 k=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 114 k-1=0 \Rightarrow k=\frac{1}{4}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the angles which a half ray makes with the positive direction of the axes, then $\sin ^2 \alpha+\sin ^2 \beta+\sin ^2 \gamma$ is equal to
questions.solution:

$\begin{array}{lr}\therefore & \cos ^2 \alpha+\cos ^2 \beta+\cos ^2 \gamma=1 \\ \Rightarrow & 1-\sin ^2 \alpha+1-\sin ^2 \beta+1-\sin ^2 \gamma=1 \\ \Rightarrow & \sin ^2 \alpha+\sin ^2 \beta+\sin ^2 \gamma=2\end{array}$

questions.q: The direction cosines $I, m, n$ of two lines are connected by the relations $l+m+n=0\mathrm{lm}=0$, then the angle between them is
questions.solution:
Given, $1+m+n=0$\ldots(i)
and $\operatorname{lm}=0$
Either $m=0 \text { or } l=0$
If $l=0$, then put in Eq. (i), we get $m=-n\therefore$ Direction ratios are $0,-n, n$ i.e. $0,-1,1$
If $m=0$, then put in Eq. (i), we get $l=-n\therefore$ Direction ratios are $-n, 0, n$ i.e. $-1,0,1\therefore \cos \theta=\frac{0 \times(-1)+(-1) \times 0+1 \times 1}{\sqrt{(0)^2+(-1)^2+(1)^2} \sqrt{(-1)^2+(0)^2+(1)^2}}=\frac{1}{2}\Rightarrow \quad \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$

questions.q: The equation of the plane passing through the line of intersection of the planes $x+y+z=6$ and $2 x+3 y+4 z+5=0$ and perpendicular to the plane $4 x+5 y-3 z=8$ is
questions.solution:
The intersection of two planes is
$\begin{aligned} & (x+y+z-6)+\lambda(2 x+3 y+4 z+5)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow(1+2 \lambda) x+(1+3 \lambda) y+(1+4 \lambda) z+(-6+5 \lambda)=0\ldots(i)\end{aligned}$ 
Since, this plane is perpendicular to the plane
$4 x+5 y-3 z-8=0\therefore \quad(1+2 \lambda) 4+(1+3 \lambda) 5+(1+4 \lambda)(-3)=0\Rightarrow \quad \lambda=\frac{-6}{11}$
On putting the value of $\lambda$ in Eq. (i), we get
$\left(-\frac{1}{11}\right) x+\left(-\frac{7}{11}\right) y+\left(-\frac{13}{11}\right) z+\left(-\frac{96}{11}\right)=0\Rightarrow \quad x+7 y+13 z+96=0$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The vector equation of the plane through the point $\hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ and perpendicular to the line of intersection of the plane $\mathbf{r} \cdot(3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})=1$ and $\mathbf{r} \cdot(\hat{\mathbf{i}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{k}})=2$ is
questions.solution:
The line of intersection of the planes $\mathbf{r} \cdot(3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})=1$ and $\mathbf{r} \cdot(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}})=2$ is common to both the planes.
Therefore, it is perpendicular to normals to the two planes i.e. $\mathbf{n}_1=3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ and $\mathbf{n}_2=\hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$. Hence, it is parallel to the vector
$\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2=-2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+7 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+13 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$
Thus, we have to find the equation of the plane passing through $\mathbf{a}=\hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ and normal to the vector $\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{n}_1 \times \mathbf{n}_2$.
The equation of the required plane is
$(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{n}$ or $\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n}=\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{n}$
or $\mathbf{r} \cdot(-2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+7 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+13 \hat{\mathbf{k}})=(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}) \cdot(-2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+7 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+13 \hat{\mathbf{k}})$
or $\mathbf{r} \cdot(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-7 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-13 \hat{\mathbf{k}})=1$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The image of the point $P(1,3,4)$ in the plane $2 x-y+z+3=0$, is
questions.solution:
We know that, the image of the point $\left(x_1, y_1, z_1\right)$ in the plane $a x+b y+c z+d=0$ is given by
$\begin{aligned} \frac{x-x_1}{a} & =\frac{y-y_1}{b}=\frac{z-z_1}{c} \\ & =\frac{-2\left(a x_1+b y_1+c z_1+d\right)}{a^2+b^2+c^2}\end{aligned}$
So, the image of the point $P(1,3,4)$ in the plane $2 x-y+z+3=0$ is given by
$\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-3}{-1}=\frac{z-4}{1}=\frac{-2(2-3+4+3)}{4+1+1}\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-3}{-1}=\frac{z-4}{1}=-2 \\ \Rightarrow & x=-3, y=5, z=2\end{array}$
Hence, the required point is $(-3,5,2)$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Equation of the plane that contains the lines $\mathbf{r}=(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}})+\lambda(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}})$
and $\mathbf{r}=(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}})+\mu(-\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}})$, is
questions.solution:
The lines are parallel to the vectors $\mathbf{b}_1=\hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ and $\mathbf{b}_2=-\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$.
$\therefore$ The plane normal to the vector $\mathbf{n}$ is
$\mathbf{b}_1 \times \mathbf{b}_2=\left|\begin{array}{rrr}\hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & -2\end{array}\right|=-3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$
The required plane passes through $(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}})$ and is normal to the vector $\mathbf{n}$.
$\therefore$ Its equation is
$\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n}=\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{n}\begin{array}{lc}\Rightarrow & \mathbf{r} \cdot(-3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}})=(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}) \cdot(-3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}}) \\ \Rightarrow & \mathbf{r} \cdot(-3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}})=-3+3 \\ \Rightarrow & \quad \mathbf{r} \cdot(-\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})=0\end{array}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The distance of the point $(3,8,2)$ from the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z-2}{3}$ measured parallel to the plane $3 x+2 y-2 z+15=0$, is
questions.solution:
Let $P(3,8,2)$ be the given point. Let the equation of a line through $P(3,8,2)$ and parallel to the plane $3 x+2 y-2 z+15=0$ be $\frac{x-3}{a}=\frac{y-8}{b}=\frac{z-2}{c}$ ...(i)
Then, normal to the plane is perpendicular to the parallel line. Then, $3 a+2 b-2 c=0$ Line (i) intersects the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z-2}{3}$ at ...(ii) Line (i) intersects the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z-2}{3}$ at $Q$. $\therefore \quad\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 3-1 & 8-3 & 2-2 \\ a & b & c \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \end{array}\right|=0\Rightarrow \quad\left|\begin{array}{lll}2 & 5 & 0 \\ a & b & c \\ 2 & 4 & 3\end{array}\right|=0\Rightarrow \quad 2(3 b-4 c)-5(3 a-2 c)=0\Rightarrow \quad 15 a-6 b-2 c=0$ (iii) On solving Eqs. (ii) and (iii) by cross-multiplication, we get $\frac{a}{-4-12}=\frac{b}{-30+6}=\frac{c}{-18-30}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{a}{-16}=\frac{b}{-24}=\frac{c}{-48} \Rightarrow \frac{a}{2}=\frac{b}{3}=\frac{c}{6}$ Substituting $a, b$ and $c$ in Eq. (i), we get $\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-8}{3}=\frac{z-2}{6}=\lambda$ [say] Let the coordinates of $Q$ be $(2 \lambda+3,3 \lambda+8,6 \lambda+2)$. It lies on the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z-2}{3}\therefore \quad \lambda+1=\frac{3 \lambda+5}{4}=2 \lambda\Rightarrow \quad \lambda=1\therefore$ Coordinate of $Q=(2+3,3+8,6+2)$ i.e. $Q=(5,11,8)$. Hence, $\begin{aligned} P Q & =\sqrt{(5-3)^2+(11-8)^2+(8-2)^2} \\ & =\sqrt{4+9+36}=7\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: A vector perpendicular to the plane containing the points $A(1,-1,2), B(2,0,-1)$, $C(0,2,1)$ is
questions.solution:
We know that a vector perpendicular to the plane containing the point $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ is given by $\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B}+\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{C}+\mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{A}$.
Given, $\mathbf{A}=\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}, \quad=2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+0 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}$
and $\mathbf{C}=0 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}$
Now, $\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B}=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}\hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & -1\end{array}\right|=\hat{\mathbf{i}}+5 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{C}=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}\hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\ 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{array}\right|=2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{A}=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}\hat{\mathbf{i}} & \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2\end{array}\right|=5 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$
Thus, $\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B}+\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{C}+\mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{A}\begin{aligned} & =(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+5 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{k}})+(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{k}})+(5 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}) \\ & =8 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The equation of the plane through the intersection of the planes $x+y+z=1$ and $2 x+3 y-z+4=0$ and parallel to $X$-axis, is
questions.solution:
The equation of the plane through the intersection of the planes $x+y+z=1$ and $2 x+3 y-z+4=0$ is
$(x+y+z-1)+\lambda(2 x+3 y-z+4)=0$
or $(2 \lambda+1) x+(3 \lambda+1) y+(1-\lambda) z+4 \lambda-1=0 \ldots$ ...(i)
It is parallel to $X$-axis.
i.e.
$\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y}{0}=\frac{z}{0}\begin{array}{ll}\therefore & 1(2 \lambda+1)+0 \times(3 \lambda+1)+0(1-\lambda)=0 \\ \Rightarrow & \lambda=-\frac{1}{2}\end{array}
On substituting $\lambda=-\frac{1}{2}$ in Eq. (i), we get
$\begin{array}{r}\left(2 x-\frac{1}{2}+1\right) x+\left(3 \times \frac{-1}{2}+1\right) y+\left(1+\frac{1}{2}\right) \\ z+4 \times\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)-1=0\end{array}
$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow & \frac{-1}{2} y+\frac{3}{2} z-3 \\ = & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & y-3 z+6\end{aligned}=0$
which is the equation of the required plane.

questions.q: The line joining the points $(1,1,2)$ and $(3,-2,1)$ meets the plane $3 x+2 y+z=6$ at the point
questions.solution:
The straight line joining the points $(1,1,2)$ and $(3,-2,1)$ is $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{-3}=\frac{z-2}{-1}=r$(say)
$\therefore$ point is $(2 r+1,1-3 r, 2-r)$ which lies on $3 x+2 y+z=6\therefore \quad 3(2 r+1)+2(1-3 r)+2-r=6\Rightarrow \quad r=1$ So, required point is $(3,-2,1)$.

questions.q: The image of the point with position vector $\hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$ in the plane $\mathbf{r} \cdot(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})=1$ is
questions.solution:
Let $Q$ be the image of the point $P(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}})$ in the plane $r \cdot(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})=1$. Then $P Q$ is normal to the plane. Since $P Q$ passes through $P$ and is normal to the given plane, therefore equation of $P Q$ is
$\mathbf{r}=(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}})+\lambda(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})$
Since, $Q$ lies on the line $P Q$, so, let the position vector of $Q$ be $(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}})+\lambda(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})\Rightarrow(1+\lambda) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+\lambda \hat{\mathbf{j}}+(3+\lambda) \hat{\mathbf{k}}$
Since $R$ is the mid point of $P Q$, therefore position vector of $R$ is $\begin{aligned} & \frac{(1+\lambda) \mathbf{i}+\lambda \mathbf{j}+(3+\lambda) \hat{\mathbf{k}}+\hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}}}{2} \\ & \text { or }\left(\frac{\lambda+2}{2}\right) \mathbf{i}+\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right) \hat{\mathbf{j}}+\left(3+\frac{\lambda}{2}\right) \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\ & \text { or }\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}+1\right) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right) \hat{\mathbf{j}}+\left(3+\frac{\lambda}{2}\right) \hat{\mathbf{k}} \end{aligned}$
Since, $R$ less on the plane r$\cdot(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})=1$ Therefore, $\begin{array}{ll} {\left[\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}+1\right) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right) \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\left(3+\frac{\lambda}{2}\right) \hat{\mathbf{k}}\right] \cdot(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}})} & =1 \\ \Rightarrow \left(\frac{\lambda}{2}+1+\frac{\lambda}{2}+3+\frac{\lambda}{2}\right) \\ \Rightarrow \lambda=-2 \end{array} \\ So, the position vector of $Q$ is $(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}})-2(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}})=-\hat{\mathbf{i}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}

questions.q: The equation of the plane through the intersection of the planes $3 x-y+2 z-4=0$ and $x+y+z-2=0$ and the point $(2,2,1)$ is
questions.solution:
The equation of any plane through the intersection of the planes, $3 x-y+2 z-4=0$ and $x+y+z-2=0$, is $(3 x-y+2 z-4)+\lambda(x+y+z-2)=0$...(i)
The plane passes through the point $(2,2,1)$. Therefore, this point will satisfy Eq. (i). $\begin{array}{cc} \therefore & (3 \times 2-2+2 \times 1-4)+\lambda(2+2+1-2)=0 \\ \Rightarrow & (6-4)+3 \lambda=0 \\ \Rightarrow & 2+3 \lambda=0 \\ \Rightarrow & \lambda=\frac{-2}{3} \end{array} On substituting this value of $\lambda$ in Eq. (i), we get the required plane as $\begin{array}{rr} (3 x-y+2 z-4)-\frac{2}{3}(x+y+z-2)=0 \\ \Rightarrow 9 x-3 y+6 z-12-2 x-2 y-2 z+4=0 \\ \Rightarrow 7 x-5 y+4 z-8=0 \end{array}
This is the required equation of the plane.

questions.q: If the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the point $(2,0,1)$ on a line passing through $(\alpha, 5,1)$ is $\left(\frac{7}{3}, \frac{5}{3}, \frac{15}{4}\right)$, then $\alpha$ is equal to_____

questions.q: If $\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{3}, n\right)$ are the direction cosines of a line, then the value of $n$ is
questions.solution: Since, $\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{3}, n\right)$ are the direction cosines of a line, then $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2+\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2+n^2=1 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{9}+n^2=1\Rightarrow n^2=1-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}=\frac{23}{36} \Rightarrow n=\frac{\sqrt{23}}{6}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The equation of plane passing through a point $A(2,-1,3)$ and parallel to the vectors $\mathbf{a}=(3,0,-1)$ and $\mathbf{b}=(-3,2,2)$ is
questions.solution:
Since, plane is parallel to a given vector, it implies that normal of plane must perpendicular to the given vectors. Given point to which plane passes through is $(2,-1,3)$. Let $A, B$ and $C$ are direction ratios of its normal.
$\therefore$ Equation of plane is
$A(x-2)+B(y+1)+C(z-3)=0$
Now, normal to plane $A \mathbf{i}+B \mathbf{j}+C \mathbf{k}$ is perpendicular to the given vectors
and $\quad \begin{aligned} & \mathbf{a}=3 \mathbf{i}+0 \mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k} \\ & \mathbf{b}=-3 \mathbf{i}+2 \mathbf{j}+2 \mathbf{k}\end{aligned}\therefore \quad 3 A+0 B-C=0$..(i)
and $\quad-3 A+2 B+2 C=0$..(ii)
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$\frac{A}{2}=\frac{B}{-3}=\frac{C}{6}\therefore$ Equation of plane be
$\begin{array}{ll} & 2(x-2)-3(y+1)+6(z-3)=0 \\ \text { i.e., } \quad & 2 x-3 y+6 z-25=0\end{array}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The locus of the equation $x y+y z=0$ is
questions.solution:
$x y+y z=0 \Leftrightarrow(x+z) y=0 \Leftrightarrow y=0$
or $x+z=0$
The equations $y=0$ and $x+z=0$ represents planes which are at right angles as their altitudes numbers are $ \lt 0,1,0\gt$ and $\langle 1,0,1\rangle$ respectively.

Hence, the line $P Q$ and $R S$ intersect.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The image of the point with position vector $i+3 \mathbf{k}$ in the plane $r \cdot(i+j+k)=1$ is
questions.solution:
Let $Q$ be the image of the point $P(\mathbf{i}+3 \mathrm{k})$ in the plane $\mathbf{r} \cdot(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})=1$. Then, $P Q$ is normal to the plane. Since, $P Q$ passes through $P$ and in normal to the oiven plane, therefore equation of $P Q$ is $\mathbf{r}=(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{)}+\lambda(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})$
Since, $Q$ lies on the line $P Q$, so let the position vector of $Q$ be $(\mathbf{i}+3 \mathbf{k})+\lambda(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})$ i.e., $(1+\lambda) \mathbf{i}+\lambda \mathbf{j}+(3+\lambda) \mathbf{k}$. Since, $R$ is the mid-point of $P Q$, therefore position vector of $R$ is $\begin{aligned} & \frac{(1+\lambda) \mathbf{i}+\lambda \mathbf{j}+(3+\lambda) \mathbf{k}+\mathbf{i}+3 \mathbf{k}}{2} \\ & =\left(\frac{\lambda+2}{2}\right) \mathbf{i}+\frac{\lambda}{2} \mathbf{j}+\left(\frac{6+\lambda}{2}\right) \mathbf{k} \\ & =\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}+1\right) \mathbf{i}+\frac{\lambda}{2} \mathbf{j}+\left(3+\frac{\lambda}{2}\right) \mathbf{k}\end{aligned}$ Since, $R$ lies on the plane $\mathbf{r} \cdot(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})=1\therefore \quad\left[\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}+1\right) \mathbf{i}+\frac{\lambda}{2} \mathbf{j}+\left(3+\frac{\lambda}{2}\right) \mathbf{k}\right]\cdot(\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})=1\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad\left[\frac{\lambda}{2}+1+\frac{\lambda}{2}+3+\frac{\lambda}{2}\right]=1 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \lambda=-2\end{aligned}$ Hence, the position vector of $Q$ is $-\mathbf{i}-2 \mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}$.

questions.q: Equation of a plane passing through $(-1,1,1)$ and $(1,-1,1)$ and perpendicular to $x+2 y+2 z=5$ is
questions.solution:
Equation of plane passing through $(-1,1,1)$ is
$a(x+1)+b(y-1)+c(z-1)=0$  ....(i)
Also, it is passing through $(1,-1,1)$.
$\therefore \quad a(1+1)+b(-1-1)+c(1-1)=0\Rightarrow \quad 2 a-2 b+0 c=0$  ....(ii)
Also, required equation of plane
(i) is perpendicular to $x+2 y+2 z=5$.
$\therefore \quad a \times 1+b \times 2+c \times 2=0\Rightarrow \quad a+2 b+2 c=0$
Eqs. (ii) and (iii) are identical.
$\therefore \quad \frac{a}{-4-0}=\frac{-b}{4-0}=\frac{c}{4+2}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{a}{-4}=\frac{b}{-4}=\frac{c}{6}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{a}{-2}=\frac{b}{-2}=\frac{c}{3}=\lambda$ (say)
$\Rightarrow \quad a=-2 \lambda, b=-2 \lambda, c=3 \lambda$
On putting the values of $a, b$ and $c$ in Eq. (i), we get
$-2 \lambda(x+1)-2 \lambda(y-1)+3 \lambda(z-1)=0\Rightarrow \quad \lambda[-2 x-2-2 y+2+3 z-3]=0\Rightarrow \quad-2 x-2 y+3 z-3=0\Rightarrow \quad 2 x+2 y-3 z+3=0$
